blocks.prompt: The Doctor Who Listens
blocks.text: A doctor's job is to find out what is happening inside you. That is hard, because you are not see-through. So the doctor uses tools. The stethoscope lets her hear your heart. Lub-dub. Lub-dub. Those sounds are little doors inside your heart closing. The doors open to let blood through, then snap shut. A healthy heart beats about one hundred thousand times every day. You never have to think about it. The doctor listens, counts, and nods. Everything sounds right.

blocks.prompt: A Tube Made of Paper
blocks.text: In 1816, a doctor in Paris named Rene Laennec had a problem. To hear a patient's heart, a doctor had to press an ear straight onto the person's chest. It was awkward. It did not work well on everyone. One day Laennec remembered a game he had watched children play. They scratched one end of a long wooden beam, and a friend at the other end could hear the scratch travel through the wood. Laennec rolled a sheet of paper into a tight tube. He put one end on his patient's chest and the other end at his ear. The heartbeat came through louder and clearer than he had ever heard it. Later he built a better version out of wood. He named it the stethoscope, from two Greek words meaning chest and examine. Doctors still use it today, more than two hundred years later. It is the tool you picture when you picture a doctor.

blocks.prompt: The Man Who Turned Listening Into Looking
blocks.text: Doctors have always had the same problem: the body keeps its secrets on the inside. For most of history, a doctor could look at your skin, feel your pulse, and ask how you felt. Everything else was guesswork. Rene Laennec changed that in Paris in 1816. Listening to a heart meant pressing an ear directly against a patient's chest, which was uncomfortable for everyone and nearly useless on larger patients. Laennec remembered watching children send sound along a wooden beam, one scratching an end while another listened. He rolled a sheet of paper into a tube, set it on his patient's chest, and leaned in. The heart arrived with startling clarity. He spent the next three years turning the paper tube into wood and, more importantly, cataloging what came through it. Crackles. Wheezes. Murmurs. Rattles. He learned to match each sound to what he later found inside the body, and he wrote it all down so other doctors could learn the same language. He called the device the stethoscope, from the Greek stethos, meaning chest, and skopein, meaning to examine. The name is exact. He had turned listening into a way of seeing. There is a hard ending. Laennec spent his career listening to the ruined lungs of patients with tuberculosis, a disease that was everywhere in Paris and that nobody could cure. In 1826 he grew ill himself. His nephew examined him with a stethoscope, the instrument his uncle had invented, and heard tuberculosis in his chest. Laennec died that year at forty-five.

blocks.prompt: The Doctor Nobody Wanted to Believe
blocks.text: In 1847, the Vienna General Hospital ran two maternity clinics side by side, taking women on alternating days. The clinics looked identical. They were not. In the first clinic, staffed by doctors and medical students, roughly one mother in ten died of a fever that swept the ward. In the second, staffed by midwives, the number was closer to one in twenty-five. Women in Vienna knew the difference. Some begged to be admitted to the second clinic. Some gave birth in the street rather than take their chances in the first. Ignaz Semmelweis, a young doctor working there, could not let the puzzle go. Same building. Same air. Same food. Same women. The only real difference was who delivered the babies, and what those people had been doing beforehand. The doctors and students spent their mornings dissecting bodies in the autopsy room, then walked upstairs to examine mothers. The midwives did not. That spring, a colleague of his, Jakob Kolletschka, cut his finger with a student's scalpel during an autopsy and died. Semmelweis read the report of Kolletschka's illness and recognized it: it was the same disease killing the mothers. Something invisible was traveling from the dead to the living on doctors' hands. Germs had not been discovered yet, so Semmelweis had no name for it. He called it cadaverous particles. He ordered every doctor to scrub with a chlorinated lime solution before entering the ward. Deaths in the first clinic collapsed within months, from roughly one in ten to about one in fifty. It should have made him famous. Instead it made him hated. His claim carried an insult inside it: that respectable doctors had been carrying death on their own hands. Colleagues mocked him. The hospital did not renew his position. He grew angrier and less careful with his arguments, and in 1865 he was committed to an asylum, where he died at forty-seven of an infected wound. Within two decades, Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister proved that germs cause disease, and the handwashing Semmelweis had begged for became ordinary. He was right, and being right did not save him.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Laennec, 1816: sound (the stethoscope)
Semmelweis, 1847: the invisible on our hands
Rontgen, 1895: X-rays, the first look at living bone
Rontgen refused to patent his discovery
He won the first Nobel Prize in Physics, 1901
Each advance was resisted before it was adopted

blocks.prompt: Learning to See Inside a Person
blocks.text: A doctor's central problem has never changed: a patient can tell you where it hurts, but not why. The body keeps its business behind skin. For most of recorded history a physician worked from the outside only, reading the surface for clues and guessing at the rest. The history of medicine is largely the history of finding ways to perceive what the body hides, and of the arguments those ways started. The first breakthrough was sound. In 1816, Rene Laennec, a physician in Paris, needed to hear a patient's heart. The method of the day was to lay an ear directly on the chest, which was awkward and often useless. Laennec recalled watching children play with a wooden beam, one child scratching one end while another listened at the far end as the sound carried cleanly through the wood. He rolled a sheet of paper into a tight cylinder, placed one end on the chest, and put his ear to the other. The heart arrived louder than he had ever heard it. Over the next three years he refined the tube into turned wood and, more importantly, built a vocabulary for what came through it: crackles, wheezes, murmurs, rattles. He matched each sound to the damage he later found inside the body, and he published the pairings so that any doctor could learn them. He named the device the stethoscope, from the Greek stethos, chest, and skopein, to examine. The name is precise. He had converted listening into a form of looking. The second breakthrough was not a device but a fact nobody wanted. In 1847, at the Vienna General Hospital, Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that mothers in the clinic run by doctors died of fever at several times the rate of mothers in the clinic run by midwives. The buildings, the air, and the patients were the same. The hands were not: the doctors came to the ward straight from the autopsy room. When a colleague died after cutting himself during a dissection, of what Semmelweis recognized as the same disease, he concluded that something invisible rode from the dead to the living on physicians' hands. He ordered scrubbing with chlorinated lime, and deaths fell by roughly ninety percent. His reward was ridicule and dismissal. The finding was correct and unbearable, because it named doctors as the cause, and it arrived before germ theory existed to explain it. Semmelweis died in an asylum in 1865. Pasteur and Lister vindicated him within twenty years, which was twenty years too late for him and for a great many mothers. The third breakthrough made the hidden literally visible. On a November evening in 1895, Wilhelm Rontgen was working with a covered vacuum tube in Wurzburg when a screen across the room began to glow. Something was passing through the cardboard. He worked for weeks in near secrecy, then photographed his wife's hand: bones, dark and exact, with her wedding ring floating around a finger. She is said to have looked at the image and answered, I have seen my death. Rontgen called the unknown rays X. He refused to patent them, on the grounds that they belonged to everyone. Within a year, doctors on several continents were photographing fractures and bullets. Three problems, three answers, one shape. Each advance let doctors perceive something the body had kept private, and each met resistance in proportion to how much it asked the profession to change its habits. Laennec's tube was dismissed by physicians who preferred to trust their own bare ears. Semmelweis was destroyed. Rontgen, who threatened nobody's pride, was handed the first Nobel Prize in Physics. The pattern is worth remembering. The evidence usually arrives before the profession is ready to accept what it costs.
